expansion:
Posterior capsular opacification is correct. This is the typical late complication after cataract extraction with IOL implantation: the lecture states that it occurs "Months–years" after surgery and is the "Most common late complication" (L18, page 16). Lens epithelial cells "migrate on the posterior capsule → 'after-cataract'", producing an opacity behind the implanted IOL and a gradual return of blurred vision (L18, page 18). The two-year gradual course and fibrotic posterior capsular opacity therefore fit PCO. The lecture gives Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy as definitive outpatient treatment (L18, page 16).

Endophthalmitis is wrong because it is an infective, vision-threatening postoperative complication with a much earlier presentation: "24–72 hrs (acute) or weeks (delayed)" (L18, page 18). Its listed signs are pain, redness, reduced VA, hypopyon, and yellowish vitreous haze, rather than an isolated dense opacity behind the IOL (L18, page 16).

Retinal detachment is wrong because the lecture identifies it as a higher-risk complication when there has been posterior capsule rupture with vitreous loss (L18, page 16); this operation was uncomplicated. Retinal detachment involves separation of the neurosensory retina and typically causes flashes, floaters, or a curtain-like visual-field defect rather than a posterior capsular opacity behind an IOL (not taken from the course material).

Cystoid macular edema is wrong because it occurs "Weeks–months" after surgery and represents fluid accumulating in the macular Henle's layer (L18, page 16). It is diagnosed by OCT showing a "petaloid fluid pattern," not by a fibrotic opacity behind the IOL (L18, page 18).
objective: Recognize posterior capsular opacification as the common late cause of recurrent gradual visual blurring after cataract surgery with IOL implantation.
